question_en: A foreigner is staying in my homestay. Do I have to tell the police or government?
answer: Yes, if you take foreign guests for a stay. Under the Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025 (in force since 1 September 2025) the keeper of the accommodation, which includes homestays, must send the guest's details on Form-III (earlier called Form C) within 24 hours of arrival. It is sent online on indianfrro.gov.in or in the Indian Visa Su-Swagatam mobile app.
actions: Ask every foreign guest, including OCI card holders, for passport and visa details when they arrive.
Submit Form-III online within 24 hours of arrival and save the acknowledgement.
Ask your District Tourism Office or local police to help you register on the portal if you are new to it.
caution: Rules and forms can change. This answer is taken from a state government notice and news reports that quote the central Rules; the Gazette text was not opened.
context_needed: do you already have a portal login
evidence: Nagaland govt notice (S80) quotes Sec 8(1) of the Act and Rule 17(5): Form-III within 24 hours via indianfrro.gov.in or Su-Swagatam app; S82 cites MHA notification 01.09.2025
verify_with: District Tourism Office / local police station / FRRO (indianfrro.gov.in)

question_en: Do I also have to report when the foreign guest leaves? What records must I keep?
answer: Reports say you must also record the guest's departure date, time and next destination, and keep these records on computer for at least one year. Guests should sign the record. Police, the district magistrate or the Registration Officer can ask to see the records.
actions: Write the departure date, time and next address in the record when the guest leaves.
Keep the Form-III acknowledgements and register safe for at least one year.
Show the records politely when an officer asks and ask for the officer's name.
caution: Reports differ on whether departure also needs a separate online entry within 24 hours. Confirm this on the portal or with the FRRO.
evidence: S80: records kept electronically at least one year, inspection by Registration Officer, DM or police not below Head Constable; S82: arrival and departure within 24 hours
verify_with: District Tourism Office / local police station / FRRO (indianfrro.gov.in)

question_en: Police will punish me if a foreigner stays without papers or I forget to report?
answer: Notices from district officers say that failing to report foreign guests can lead to penal action under the Immigration and Foreigners Act 2025. The exact fine or jail term was not verified here, so do not guess. The easy protection is to report on time and keep proof.
actions: Report every foreign guest within 24 hours and keep the acknowledgement.
Report late rather than never, and tell the police or FRRO honestly why it was late.
Ask a lawyer or the district legal services authority if an FIR has already been filed against you.
caution: This is not legal advice. Do not hide a foreign guest from officers.
evidence: S80 and S81 say non-compliance invites penal action; no penalty amounts verified
verify_with: Local police / lawyer / District Legal Services Authority

question_en: My homestay is part of my family house. Is it still counted as 'accommodation' for foreigner reporting?
answer: Reports list homestays among places that must report. One explainer says a purely non-commercial family residence may be treated differently, but this was not verified on the Act's text. If you take paying foreign guests, the safe step is to report them.
actions: Report paying foreign guests on Form-III.
Ask the FRRO or local police in writing whether your case is treated differently.
Keep a copy of the answer.
caution: Do not assume you are exempt. Ask the authority before relying on any exemption.
evidence: S80/S81 list homestays among accommodation providers; the exemption claim was seen only in one secondary explainer and was not verified
verify_with: District Tourism Office / local police station / FRRO (indianfrro.gov.in)

question_en: A foreign guest says they lost their passport or has no papers. Can I still give a room?
answer: Form-III needs the guest's identity and visa details, so you cannot complete it without them. Do not hide the guest or send them away at night. Call the local police or the FRRO for advice and note the time and what the guest told you.
actions: Ask politely to see the passport or any police report of loss.
Call the local police station for advice before giving a room.
Write down the guest's name, nationality and the time you called.
caution: Safety first: do not leave a foreign guest without shelter at night. Exact procedure for lost passports was not verified.
evidence: S80 says foreigners must provide particulars; lost-passport handling not verified
verify_with: Local police / FRRO / the guest's embassy

question_en: Do I need to take ID from Indian guests and keep a register?
answer: A guest register with name, address, phone, ID type, arrival and departure is a normal and safe practice. Some states or tourism departments make it compulsory for registered homestays, but this was not verified for any state here. Ask your District Tourism Office what applies to you.
actions: Keep a bound or digital register of all guests with arrival and departure dates.
Look at a government photo ID and note only the type and last digits unless the law needs more.
Ask your District Tourism Office or police whether your state has a format.
caution: Do not photocopy IDs unless needed. See the data privacy rows for storage.
evidence: No state rule verified; method given

question_en: An Indian guest has no ID card. Should I refuse the room?
answer: There is no national rule found here that tells small hosts to refuse every guest without ID. Many hosts ask for any photo ID, such as voter card, driving licence or a photo on a phone. If the guest has no ID and seems unsafe, you can decline or call the police for advice. Your state's rule may be stricter.
actions: Ask politely for any photo ID and phone number and write it in the register.
Decline or call the police if the guest refuses to give any details and something feels wrong.
Never ask for ID in a way that insults the guest.
caution: State and local police rules vary. Verify before making a firm policy.
verify_with: Local police station / District Tourism Office

question_en: What should I do if police come to check my guest register?
answer: Officers named in the foreigners rules (Registration Officer, District Magistrate or police not below Head Constable) can ask for your records of foreign guests. Stay calm, be polite and show the register and Form-III acknowledgements. Ask the officer for name and rank.
actions: Keep the register and acknowledgements in one place that you can reach quickly.
Show only the records that the officer asks for.
Write down the date, officer's name and what was asked.
caution: This is general guidance, not legal advice.
evidence: Inspection powers as quoted in S80 and S81 (Rule 17(1))

question_en: My village is in the northeast. Does a foreign guest need a Protected Area Permit?
answer: A Protected Area Permit is a special permit for foreigners in some border areas under the Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order 1958. Reports say MHA relaxed it in Manipur, Nagaland and Mizoram for years but reimposed it from December 2023. Another report said Mizoram had not started enforcing it by December 2024. The current position is unclear.
actions: Ask the guest to check with the FRRO, an Indian mission or the state tourism department before travel.
Do not promise permits to the guest.
Ask your District Tourism Office what permit your area needs now.
caution: Conflicting reports. This Order was made under an older law, so ask what replaced it. Never advise foreigners to enter without checking.
scope: Northeast states (Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal and others)
evidence: S83 reports MHA reimposing the regime from Dec 2023; S85 describes PAP (data as of 2018); status disputed
verify_with: FRRO / State Home or Tourism Department / MHA

question_en: Do Indian tourists need a permit to come to my village in Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal or Manipur?
answer: Yes. Indian citizens who live outside these four states need an Inner Line Permit (ILP) to enter Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland and Manipur. Each state issues its own, and many have online application. Validity and fees differ by state and change, so check the state website.
actions: Tell guests to apply for the ILP before they travel.
Check the state's official ILP site for the current fee and validity.
Ask for a copy or photo of the ILP at check-in if your state expects it.
caution: Whether hosts must check the ILP is not verified. Ask the local administration. People from the state itself do not need it.
evidence: S84 explainer; fees and validity not repeated
verify_with: State Home Department / District Commissioner's office

topic: Restricted Area Permit Sikkim Ladakh Andaman
question_en: My foreign guest wants to go to a border area in Sikkim, Ladakh or Andaman. Who gets the permit?
answer: Parts of Sikkim, Ladakh and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands have been listed as Restricted Areas for foreigners, who need a Restricted Area Permit. The guest or their travel agent normally applies, not the village host. In 2018 about 30 inhabited Andaman islands were taken out of RAP; current status was not verified.
actions: Tell the guest to ask their travel agent or the tourism department about the permit before coming.
Do not take foreign guests to border or restricted spots without written permission.
Ask the District Tourism Office for the current list of areas.
caution: Rules change and differ between Sikkim, Ladakh and Andaman. Treat this as a pointer only.
verify_with: State Tourism Department / FRRO / District Administration

question_en: My homestay is not registered with the Tourism Department. Can I still take foreign guests?
answer: Foreigner reporting is a separate duty and applies even if you have no tourism registration, according to the reports read. Many states have homestay schemes and some limit who may take guests, but this was not verified here. Ask your District Tourism Office.
actions: Report foreign guests on Form-III whatever your registration status.
Ask the District Tourism Office how to register your homestay.
Keep your own details ready (address, contact, number of rooms) for the portal.
caution: State homestay rules are not verified.
evidence: S80 duty applies to keepers of accommodation; state scheme not checked

topic: Guest overstays or suspicious foreign papers
question_en: What if a foreign guest says their visa is finished or documents look fake?
answer: Do not argue or hide the guest. Take a photo or note of what you saw if the guest allows, and call the local police or FRRO for advice. The Act has penalties for fake travel documents, so leave the checking to the authorities.
actions: Stay calm and do not accuse the guest.
Call the local police or FRRO and report what you saw.
Write down the time, guest name and passport number you recorded.
caution: Do not detain anyone. Only police can act.
evidence: General guidance; duty to report from S80

question_en: Can you give me a short list of what to do on the day a foreign guest arrives?
answer: Complete these steps on the day the guest arrives so you stay inside the 24-hour reporting limit.
actions: Check passport and visa or OCI card details and write them in your register.
Submit Form-III online within 24 hours and save the acknowledgement.
Tell the guest about your emergency numbers and the nearest hospital.
caution: Ask the guest not to travel to permit-needed areas without checking.
verify_with: District Tourism Office / local police station / FRRO (indianfrro.gov.in)

question_en: Which number do I call in an emergency in my village?
answer: Dial 112. It is the single emergency number for police, fire, health and other help, and it also covers women safety and child protection. The 112 India app has an SOS button. Each state runs its own control room, so keep local numbers written too.
actions: Write 112 and your nearest hospital and police numbers on a card at reception.
Teach family and staff to give the exact village name and a landmark when they call.
Install the 112 India app on your phone.
caution: Mobile network may be weak in hills. Note the nearest place with signal.

question_en: My guest needs tourist help or information. Is there a government tourist helpline?
answer: Yes. The Ministry of Tourism runs a 24x7 toll-free Tourist Helpline: 1363 or 1800111363. It works in 12 languages including Hindi and English. It gives travel information and helps tourists in difficulty by informing the right authority.
actions: Give guests the number 1363 in your welcome note.
Call it for a foreign guest who needs help in their own language.
Use 112 for any danger to life.
caution: 1363 is for help and information, not a replacement for 112 in an emergency.

question_en: Someone sent me a fake booking payment or I lost money on UPI. Where do I complain?
answer: Call 1930 quickly or report on cybercrime.gov.in. The portal accepts complaints on financial fraud and other cyber crime and lets you track your complaint. Call your bank at once too.
actions: Call 1930 as soon as you notice the fraud and note the complaint number.
Tell your bank to block the card or UPI ID.
Keep screenshots, phone numbers and transaction IDs.
caution: Never share OTP, PIN or UPI PIN with anyone, even a person who says they are a guest.

question_en: What numbers do I call for a woman in trouble or a child at risk?
answer: Call 112 for any immediate danger. The 112 system covers women safety and child protection. Women's helpline 181 and Childline 1098 are widely used numbers, but they were not checked on an official page in this session, so confirm them on the district notice board.
actions: Call 112 first if someone is in danger now.
Confirm 181 and 1098 with the district women and child office and display them.
Stay with the person until help arrives.
caution: Confirm helpline numbers locally before printing them.
evidence: 112 coverage read on 112.gov.in; 181 and 1098 not verified
verify_with: District Child Protection Unit / District Women and Child office

question_en: Which number brings an ambulance in my area?
answer: Dial 112 and ask for an ambulance. Many states also run 108 or 102 ambulance numbers, but which one works differs by state and was not checked here. Find the number for your block and also know the nearest health centre and road route.
actions: Ask the Block Medical Officer which ambulance number works in your village.
Write the nearest hospital, distance and road route on your emergency card.
Keep a vehicle contact who can carry a patient when the ambulance cannot reach.
caution: In remote areas an ambulance can take long. Start first aid and arrange transport early.
evidence: S94 lists health services under 112; 108/102 per state not verified
verify_with: District Health Office / Block Medical Officer

question_en: My guest went for a trek and has not come back. What do I do?
answer: Call 112 or the local police right away. Do not wait for a full day. Give the guest's name, phone, clothes, route, last time seen and photo. You can report at any police station, and under the new criminal procedure law (BNSS) police can take the information even if the place is in another station's area.
actions: Call 112 or the nearest police station and tell them what you know.
Alert the Gram Panchayat, forest guards and local guides to help search.
Keep the guest's room, bag and phone number safe for the police.
caution: Do not send untrained people into danger at night or in bad weather. Let trained teams lead.
evidence: 112 page; BNSS s173 Zero FIR per secondary source
verify_with: Local police / forest department / District Disaster Management Authority

question_en: A guest's phone was stolen. How do I help them make a police complaint?
answer: Under section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS, which replaced the old CrPC from July 2024) a complaint can be given at any police station (Zero FIR). It can also be given electronically, but the person must sign it within three days. The informant gets a free copy.
actions: Take the guest to the nearest police station or help them use the state police online complaint site.
Ask for the free copy of the FIR and keep it.
Help the guest with a translator or a local contact.
caution: E-FIR facilities differ by state. Check what your state police offers.
evidence: BNSS s173 as explained on S107 (secondary)
verify_with: Local police / District Legal Services Authority

question_en: Police are not taking our complaint. What can we do?
answer: Under BNSS section 173 a person refused at the station can send the information in writing to the Superintendent of Police, who can direct registration if a cognizable offence appears. Stay calm and keep records of who you met and when.
actions: Ask politely for the reason and note the officer's name.
Send a written complaint by post or email to the Superintendent of Police.
Contact the District Legal Services Authority for free advice.
caution: This is general information, not legal advice.
verify_with: District Legal Services Authority / Superintendent of Police

question_en: Guests ask for charas or ganja in my hill village. Is this allowed?
answer: No. Under the NDPS Act 1985, charas (resin) and ganja (flowers) are controlled drugs, and even a small quantity can lead to arrest. Do not sell, supply or let guests use drugs at your property. Rules for bhang (leaf preparations) differ by state, so ask before offering anything.
actions: Put a clear 'no drugs' rule in your house rules and tell guests at check-in.
Never carry, store or share guest drugs for anyone.
Call the local police if guests are dealing drugs, and do not confront them.
caution: Penalties depend on quantity and are serious. Ask a lawyer if you have a case. Do not call it 'local culture' to guests.

question_en: Can I serve or sell liquor or home brew to guests?
answer: Alcohol is controlled by state excise laws. Many states need a licence to serve or sell it, and some states ban it. Home brews such as mahua or rice beer may be allowed for home use but not for sale in many places. This was not verified for any state here.
actions: Ask the District Excise Office what your state allows before offering any alcohol.
Do not sell any alcohol without a licence.
Never serve alcohol to children.
caution: Selling without a licence can lead to criminal cases. Never drive after drinking.

question_en: Till what time can we play music or use a speaker for a cultural night?
answer: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules 2000 define night as 10 pm to 6 am. A public address system or loudspeaker should not be used at night and needs permission from police or the authority. Limits for residential areas are 55 dB(A) in the day and 45 dB(A) at night. Silence zones extend 100 m around hospitals, schools and courts.
actions: Stop loudspeakers and DJ music by 10 pm.
Ask the local police or Gram Panchayat for permission for events with speakers.
Keep drums and music inside and at low volume near sleeping guests and neighbours.
caution: This source is a state copy of the national rule. States can add their own conditions and festival exceptions. Confirm locally.
evidence: HP Environment dept PDF quoting the 2000 Rules
verify_with: State Pollution Control Board / local police

question_en: Can I let off firecrackers for a welcome or wedding for guests?
answer: The noise rules set a noise ceiling for firecrackers (125 dB(A) at 4 metres), and states and courts often add bans or timings. Firecrackers also scare animals and risk fire in thatch or wooden houses. Ask local authorities and avoid them near forest and houses.
actions: Ask the police or Gram Panchayat before any firecrackers.
Choose drums, flowers or songs for welcomes.
Keep fire buckets ready at any event with flames.
caution: State rules on firecrackers differ and change.
evidence: S101 mentions firecracker noise limit; state bans not verified

question_en: Guests want to play cards for money in my courtyard. Is that a problem?
answer: Gambling is regulated by state laws. Playing for money, especially if you host or take a share, can be an offence in many places. Rules were not verified for any state here, so do not allow betting on your premises.
actions: Set a house rule: no betting or gambling.
Ask the local police if you are unsure.
Do not take any cut or fee from games.
caution: State laws differ widely.

question_en: A guest is with a young girl who looks scared. What should I do?
answer: If you suspect danger, call 112 and tell them what you saw. Do not confront the guest. Try to speak to the young person alone and gently. Note the room, names and vehicle number.
actions: Call 112 and report what you saw and the exact location.
Keep the person safe and in sight without scaring them.
Write down the guest details and vehicle number.
caution: Child abuse reporting is a legal duty (see child protection rows).
evidence: 112 covers women safety and child protection (S94); POCSO s19 (S91)

question_en: If I see or hear that a child is being sexually abused, am I legally required to report?
answer: Yes. Section 19 of the POCSO Act says any person who fears such an offence may happen, or knows it has happened, must report to the Special Juvenile Police Unit or the local police. Under section 21, not reporting can lead to up to six months in jail, a fine or both. Children themselves are not punished for not reporting.
actions: Call 112 or the local police and report what you know.
Keep the child safe and do not question them deeply.
Do not tell the suspect or try to settle it inside the village.
caution: Section 20 (another reporting duty) was not checked; ask a lawyer or Childline whether it applies to lodges. This is not legal advice.
verify_with: Local police / District Child Protection Unit / Childline

question_en: A child told me something bad happened to them. What do I say and do?
answer: Listen calmly and believe the child. Say it is not their fault and that you will get help. Do not ask many questions or promise to keep a secret. Report to police or 112 as the law requires.
actions: Listen and stay calm. Say thank you for telling me.
Write down the child's words, date and time.
Call 112 or the police and the Childline helpline.
caution: Do not confront the suspected person or call a village meeting about it. Protect the child's name.
evidence: S91 s19 duty; handling is general practice

question_en: Can my children or village children help in the homestay or guide guests?
answer: The child labour law (the Child and Adolescent Labour Act) generally bars work by children under 14, with an exception for helping their own family after school or in holidays, as long as it is not hazardous. Adolescents (14 to 18) cannot do hazardous work. This was not read on the Act in this session. Paid work for other children as guides, porters or entertainers is risky.
actions: Do not employ children under 14 or let them handle fire, knives, heights or night work.
Let your own child help only lightly, after school, and never at the cost of school.
Ask the District Labour Office what is allowed for 14 to 18 years.
caution: Verify with the Labour Department before involving any child in paid tourism work.
evidence: Act name and general rules recalled; not verified on source

question_en: Can village children dance or perform for tourists?
answer: Short, voluntary cultural sharing with parents' consent and school time protected is a good practice. Avoid paid or late-night shows. Do not let guests give sweets, money or touch children. A trusted adult must stay with children.
actions: Get written consent from parents for each performance.
Keep shows short, daytime and never during school hours.
Stay with the children and stop if they feel uncomfortable.
caution: Labour law limits on paid work by children apply. Ask the Labour Department.

question_en: Is it okay for guests to take photos of village children?
answer: Ask a parent first, every time, and never post identifying photos of children online without their permission. Tell guests the rule at check-in. Do not allow photos of children bathing, changing or in a vulnerable state.
actions: Put a sign and a line in the house rules: ask a parent before photographing any child.
Stop guests who photograph children secretly.
Never share a child's name, school and village together online.
caution: Practice-based safeguard. Child sexual images are a serious crime.

question_en: A teenager under 18 wants to stay alone. Should I allow it?
answer: It is safest not to give a room to a child travelling alone. Ask for a parent or guardian's phone number and written consent, and call them. If the child seems to be running away or in danger, call the police or Childline.
actions: Ask the child's age and guardian contact and call the guardian.
Do not give a private room to a minor alone without guardian approval.
Call 112 or the police if the child seems lost, unsafe or has run away.
caution: Local police may have rules. Ask.

question_en: I have only three workers. Do I need a sexual harassment committee?
answer: The POSH Act 2013 protects women at work. For workplaces with fewer than ten workers there is no internal committee. The District Officer sets up a Local Committee in each district, and a woman can complain to it, including about an employer. Treat every complaint seriously.
actions: Tell women staff how to reach the Local Committee through the District Officer or women and child office.
Behave respectfully and never pressure staff.
Do not punish or threaten anyone who complains.
caution: This was read in a secondary legal text site. Ask the District Women and Child Development officer for the Local Committee's contact.
verify_with: District Officer / Local Committee / District Women and Child Development office

question_en: A male guest is harassing a girl in my kitchen. What can I do?
answer: Stop the behaviour at once and separate them. Support the woman and ask what she wants. Tell the guest to leave and call the police if there was touching or threats. Call 112 in danger.
actions: Move the woman to safety and stay with her.
Ask the guest to leave and refuse further stay.
Call 112 or the police and help her make a complaint if she wants.
caution: Do not blame the woman. Keep a written record.
evidence: 112 covers women safety (S94); rest is practice

question_en: What simple things make solo women guests feel safe in my homestay?
answer: These are practice-based tips, not legal rules. Good locks inside the room, a well-lit path, clear house rules and a host who answers calls at night make a big difference. Be clear about who may enter rooms.
actions: Fit and test an inside latch on every guest door and window.
Share the host's phone number and emergency numbers at check-in.
Arrange trusted transport and keep a record of driver details.
caution: Never enter a guest's room without knocking and permission.

question_en: A guest says someone in my family behaved badly with her. What do I do?
answer: Take it seriously. Do not argue or hide it. Separate the person from the guest, apologise, and offer to call the police. Let the guest choose. Contact the Local Committee or police if the guest asks for it.
actions: Listen and write down what she says.
Keep the accused person away from guests.
Offer to help her call 112 and complain.
caution: Protect everyone's dignity. Do not hold a village meeting about it.
evidence: Local Committee from S92; 112 from S94

question_en: I heard there is a new data protection law. Do I have to follow it now?
answer: The DPDP Rules 2025 were notified on 14 November 2025. Rules on the Data Protection Board came into effect at once, but the main duties of businesses (notice, consent, safeguards) start after 18 months, around mid-May 2027. As of October 2026, most duties have not started yet. Sources differ by a day on the dates.
actions: Start now by collecting only the data you need.
Tell guests clearly why you collect their details.
Check the date and any rules for small businesses with a CA or lawyer.
caution: Whether a tiny homestay is covered, and how, was not verified. Do not rely on this answer for compliance.
context_needed: do you collect guest data digitally
evidence: PIB document (S86); dates per S87 and conflicting by one day in another firm's note

question_en: What should I do with guest ID photocopies and passport photos?
answer: Take only what you really need, keep it locked or password-protected, and do not share it. Foreign guest records may need to be kept for at least one year under the foreigners rules, so do not delete those early. Destroy other copies when you no longer need them.
actions: Keep paper copies in a locked drawer and phone photos in a protected folder.
Do not send ID images on WhatsApp groups.
Shred copies you no longer need once any legal period is over.
caution: Retention rules for Indian guests are not verified. Ask a lawyer.
evidence: 1-year retention for foreign guests from S80; DPDP safeguards generally from S87

question_en: Can I add past guests to my WhatsApp group or send them offers?
answer: Ask each guest first. Do not add anyone to a group without permission, and stop at once if they ask. Use a broadcast list so guests do not see each other's numbers. Only send what they agreed to receive.
actions: Ask at check-out: 'May I send you news and offers on WhatsApp?'
Keep a note of who said yes and when.
Remove anyone who asks to stop.
caution: The DPDP Act is about consent, but check current rules for small businesses.
evidence: Consent notice principle in S86; practice

question_en: Can I put CCTV cameras at my homestay? Where is it not allowed?
answer: CCTV at gates, parking and common areas is common for safety. Never put cameras in rooms, bathrooms or changing places. Hidden cameras are a serious crime. Put a notice, limit who sees the footage, and delete old recordings.
actions: Fit cameras only at entrances and shared outdoor areas.
Put a notice 'CCTV in use' where guests can see it.
Save footage for a short time only and keep access with the owner.
caution: Cameras that record sound or point at neighbours' homes can cause legal problems. Ask a lawyer.

question_en: Can I put photos of guests or villagers on Instagram or my website?
answer: Ask for permission first and keep a simple record. Share only what the person agrees to. For villagers, ask the person and, for rituals or sacred places, ask the community. For children, ask a parent.
actions: Add a short consent line to the booking or check-in form.
Ask villagers before taking their photo for marketing.
Delete a photo when a person asks you to.
caution: Respect community rules about sacred or private rites. Community controls how its culture is shown.

question_en: My phone with guest details was lost or hacked. What now?
answer: Change passwords, lock the phone and tell your bank and mobile company. Report online fraud on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in. From the main DPDP duties (around mid-May 2027) larger organisations must report certain breaches to the Data Protection Board within 72 hours and tell affected people.
actions: Change passwords and log out other devices.
Report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in if money or identity may be misused.
Tell guests whose details were exposed.
caution: The 72-hour rule is described in a secondary source and may not apply to tiny hosts.
evidence: 72-hour breach rule per S87; portal S95

question_en: How much GST do I charge on my room rent?
answer: If GST applies to you, the rate on room tariff up to Rs 7,500 per room per night is 5%, and above that it is 18%. This changed on 22 September 2025 (Notification 15/2025-Central Tax (Rate)); the old 12% band is gone. The limit is per room per day and depends on the amount actually charged.
actions: Check each room's actual price per night against the Rs 7,500 limit.
Show GST separately on the bill if you are registered.
Ask a CA whether input tax credit and other rules fit your case.
caution: This is not tax advice. Rates were read in secondary sources, not the CBIC notification.
evidence: S88 and S89 report Notification 15/2025-CT(Rate) dated 17 Sept 2025
verify_with: Chartered Accountant / GST helpdesk / local GST office

question_en: Do I need GST registration for my small homestay or tours?
answer: The usual limit for service providers is Rs 20 lakh yearly turnover (Rs 10 lakh in special category states). Some suppliers must register even below this, for example some inter-state service suppliers. This was read in a secondary source and not rechecked on the GST portal.
actions: Add up your last year's income from rooms, food and tours.
Ask a CA if you are near the limit or sell through apps.
Do not charge GST on bills if you are not registered.
caution: Not tax advice. Thresholds can change.
verify_with: Chartered Accountant / GST helpdesk / local GST office

question_en: I heard small service providers can pay a simple 6% GST. Is it for me?
answer: A report says service providers with turnover up to Rs 50 lakh may opt for a composition scheme at 6% (3% CGST and 3% SGST). Whether it fits room rent or tours was not confirmed. Ask a CA before choosing.
actions: Ask a CA if your services qualify.
Compare the scheme with normal registration, including credit loss.
Keep sales records ready for the CA.
caution: Do not choose a scheme on the basis of this answer alone.
verify_with: Chartered Accountant / GST helpdesk / local GST office

question_en: Should I register my homestay as a business?
answer: Business registration (such as Udyam) and tourism or local licences are separate topics handled in other parts of this knowledge bank. In short, ask your District Industries Centre and District Tourism Office what applies. This row only points you there.
actions: Ask the District Tourism Office about homestay registration.
Ask the District Industries Centre about Udyam.
Ask a CA about GST and income tax.
caution: Not covered here.
verify_with: District Industries Centre / District Tourism Office

question_en: Do I have to give guests a bill or receipt?
answer: Give a written receipt for every payment. It protects you and the guest. A simple receipt shows date, your name and address, guest name, what was paid for, amount and mode of payment. Registered GST taxpayers must issue proper tax invoices, so ask your CA for the format.
actions: Use a receipt book with carbon copies or a phone app.
Write date, amount, nights and purpose on each receipt.
Keep your copies for your CA.
caution: Not tax advice.
verify_with: Chartered Accountant / GST helpdesk / local GST office

question_en: How do I take UPI and cash payments safely?
answer: Use only your own bank's QR code and check the credit in your bank app or SMS before saying paid. Never share your UPI PIN or OTP, and never scan a QR to receive money. If you are cheated, call 1930.
actions: Show your own QR code and verify the credit in your bank app.
Keep a daily cash and UPI record.
Call 1930 or report on cybercrime.gov.in if you are cheated.
caution: A screenshot of payment is not proof of payment.

question_en: What can I say in my listing so it is not 'misleading advertising'?
answer: The Consumer Protection Act 2019 treats misleading advertisements and unfair trade practices as wrong, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority can act. Use real photos, correct prices, and clear facts about distance, bath, food, Wi-Fi and road. Do not promise sightings of animals or views you cannot guarantee.
actions: Check every claim in your listing for truth.
State what is included and not included in the price.
Update photos when the place changes.
caution: Penalty amounts were not verified. Ask a lawyer if you receive a notice.
evidence: Act named from general knowledge; not read on source

question_en: How do I write a fair cancellation and refund policy?
answer: Write your policy before booking and tell the guest in writing. Say how much advance, when it is refundable, and what happens in landslide, floods or road closure. Keep it fair and refund promptly when you cancel.
actions: Write a short policy and send it with the booking confirmation.
Offer refund or new dates if you or the government close the road or area.
Keep proof of the policy shared.
caution: Unfair terms can be challenged under the Consumer Protection Act. Not legal advice.

question_en: A guest threatens to complain to a consumer forum. What happens?
answer: The guest can call the National Consumer Helpline on 1915 or use its portal and app. Their complaints can then go to the consumer commission of the district. Try to solve the problem first, politely and in writing, and keep your receipts and messages.
actions: Reply to the guest in writing and offer a fair fix.
Keep bills, messages and photos.
Ask the District Legal Services Authority for free advice if a case starts.
caution: Not legal advice.
evidence: S96 consumerhelpline.gov.in page read; district commission route general

question_en: What fire safety do I need in a small homestay?
answer: Basic safety: keep at least one working fire extinguisher near the kitchen and one on each floor, keep exits clear, keep matches and lamps away from thatch and curtains, and run a quick drill. The National Building Code gives fire rules by building type and height. Small buildings mostly need basics but state fire rules vary.
actions: Buy an ISI-marked extinguisher and train everyone to use it.
Keep a bucket of sand and water in the kitchen.
Show guests the exit and keep corridors clear.
caution: This is practice-based. The exact requirement, including a fire NOC, depends on your state and building. Ask your local fire station.
evidence: General practice; NBC details not read
verify_with: District Fire Officer / local fire station

question_en: Do I need a Fire NOC for my homestay?
answer: It depends on your state, building height, number of rooms and your homestay scheme. Many small buildings under 15 m are treated lightly, but rules differ. Do not guess. Ask your District Tourism Office and the local fire station in writing.
actions: Ask the fire station what your building needs.
Ask the Tourism Office if homestay registration needs a fire certificate.
Keep the reply for your records.
caution: State-specific and not verified here.
verify_with: District Fire Officer / District Tourism Office

question_en: Is my wiring safe for guests? What should I check?
answer: Old or loose wiring is a top fire risk. Ask a licensed electrician to check wiring, earthing and fit an RCCB (a switch that cuts power during shock). Use good-quality ISI-marked wires and plugs and keep wet bathrooms safe.
actions: Call a licensed electrician for a check of earthing and switches.
Fit an RCCB on the main board.
Replace damaged sockets and cables.
caution: This is practice-based. Use a licensed electrician.

question_en: What should I do if my LPG gas smells or the cylinder leaks?
answer: Do not switch lights or phones on or off. Shut the regulator, open windows and doors, take everyone outside and call your gas distributor's emergency number or 112. Keep the cylinder upright and away from heat. Check the rubber pipe often.
actions: Turn off the regulator and open windows at the first smell of gas.
Move guests outside and call the distributor or 112.
Change old rubber pipes and check them with soapy water for bubbles.
caution: Practice-based. Follow your gas company's instructions.

topic: Gas geyser and stove carbon monoxide
question_en: Is it safe to use a gas geyser or a wood or charcoal stove in a closed room?
answer: No. Gas geysers, charcoal or wood stoves and kerosene heaters can make carbon monoxide, which you cannot smell and which can kill in a closed room. Keep gas geysers outside the bathroom with outdoor venting, and never sleep with a burning stove in a closed room.
actions: Fit gas geysers outside or with a proper vent to outside.
Never leave a charcoal or wood stove burning in a sleeping room.
Tell guests that headache, dizziness or sleepiness near a stove means move to fresh air.
caution: If a guest faints near a stove, move them to fresh air and call 112.

question_en: What do I do if cooking oil catches fire?
answer: Turn off the heat if it is safe, put a lid or damp cloth over the pan and leave it. Never throw water on an oil fire. Use a suitable extinguisher. If the fire spreads, leave and call 112.
actions: Keep a pan lid or fire blanket near the stove.
Keep an extinguisher near the kitchen door.
Leave and call 112 if the fire spreads.
caution: Practice-based.

question_en: My house is old stone or mud. Is it safe for guests? What about the balcony railing?
answer: Look for wide cracks, leaning walls, rotten beams, leaks and weak stairs. Railings must be strong, firm and high enough that a child cannot fall or climb. Ask a civil engineer or the local engineer to check before taking guests, and again after earthquakes or heavy rain.
actions: Look for cracks, damp and loose rails and mend them.
Ask a civil engineer to check the roof, beams and balcony.
Close any weak room, stairs or rooftop until fixed.
caution: Practice-based. Needs an expert.

question_en: Is there government accident insurance for me and my family?
answer: Two schemes were reported: PM Suraksha Bima Yojana (about Rs 20 a year, Rs 2 lakh cover for accidental death or total disability, Rs 1 lakh partial, age 18 to 70) and PM Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (about Rs 436 a year, Rs 2 lakh for death from any cause). You enrol through a bank or post office account. These cover you, not your guests.
actions: Ask your bank for the current premium and form.
Check that your account has balance each year in May for auto-renewal.
Ask an insurer separately about cover for guests.
caution: Figures come from a secondary source and may change.

question_en: If a guest is hurt at my place, am I covered by insurance?
answer: Government accident schemes cover the person insured, not guests. Fire insurance, public liability (covering injury to guests or damage) and activity or adventure cover are commercial policies from insurers. Ask two or three insurers what they cover and exclude for a homestay.
actions: Ask an insurer for homestay fire and public liability quotes.
Read exclusions for adventure activities.
Keep guest incident records.
caution: This is neutral general information, not advice to buy a product.
evidence: Government scheme scope per S109; commercial cover general

question_en: A guest was bitten by a snake. What should I do and not do?
answer: Keep the person calm and still, remove rings and tight clothes, and immobilise the limb like a fracture. Take them at once to a hospital that has antivenom. Do not tie a tight band, cut, suck or rub the wound, and do not use herbal or traditional remedies. Do not try to catch the snake. The person should stay under observation in hospital.
actions: Call 112 or the ambulance and start moving to the hospital immediately.
Splint the limb and keep the person lying down and calm.
Tell the doctor the time of the bite and symptoms.
caution: This follows a 2016 MoHFW guideline. Do not treat at home.
evidence: MoHFW Standard Treatment Guidelines: Snake Bite, July 2016

question_en: A dog bit or scratched a guest. What first?
answer: Wash the wound with running water and soap for at least 15 minutes. Then take the person to a doctor or health centre quickly for rabies vaccine and any other treatment the doctor advises. Do not wait to see if the dog falls ill.
actions: Wash the bite with soap and water for 15 minutes.
Take the guest to the nearest health centre.
Note the animal, place and time for the doctor.
caution: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so act the same day. Ask the doctor about vaccine availability.

question_en: A guest looks very hot, confused and stops sweating. What do I do?
answer: This can be an emergency. Move the person to shade, cool the body with wet cloths and fan, give small sips of water if they are awake, and call 112 or a doctor. In heat waves stay indoors, drink plenty of water and wear hats, as in national do's and don'ts.
actions: Move the guest into shade and cool with wet cloth.
Give small sips of water only if fully awake.
Call 112 or the ambulance if confusion or fainting continues.
caution: Not a medical diagnosis. Never leave children or pets in closed vehicles.
evidence: S98 heat wave do's and don'ts; first aid steps general

question_en: A guest has headache and vomiting at high altitude. Or feels very cold and shivers. What do I do?
answer: Headache, nausea or tiredness at height may be altitude sickness. Stop going higher, rest, drink water and go down if it gets worse. Get medical help early for confusion, breathlessness at rest or loss of balance. For a very cold person, move indoors, remove wet clothes, wrap in blankets and give warm drinks if awake.
actions: Stop further ascent and let the guest rest.
Arrange a descent and call 112 or a doctor if worse.
Warm a cold person slowly with dry clothes and warm drinks.
caution: This is general first aid, not diagnosis. For official advice refer to Red Cross, NDMA or MoHFW material.
evidence: General practice; not verified on an Indian official source

question_en: We have a river, pond or well near the homestay. How do I keep guests safe?
answer: Most drowning is preventable. Fence or cover wells and ponds, never let children near water alone, and give life jackets for boating and rafting. Do not let guests swim in fast water after rain. Keep a rope and a floating object ready, and learn first aid.
actions: Cover wells and fence ponds near the house.
Tell guests which river spots are unsafe and give life jackets for boats.
Keep a rope, ring or tube at the water point.
caution: Do not jump in to save someone unless trained. Call 112.
evidence: Practice-based (WHO drowning guidance read but not cited here)

question_en: Several guests have vomiting and loose motions after dinner. What now?
answer: Give small sips of clean water or ORS and stop serving the suspected food. Take anyone with blood in stool, high fever, weakness, severe pain, or a child, elderly or pregnant guest to a doctor. Keep leftovers aside for the health officer and tell your District Food Safety Officer.
actions: Give ORS and clean water in small sips.
Take weak or high-risk guests to a doctor.
Keep samples of the food and note what was served.
caution: Not a diagnosis. Call 112 if someone is seriously ill.

question_en: There was a road accident with guests in my vehicle. What should I do?
answer: Stop in a safe place, switch off the engine and call 112 for police and ambulance. Give first aid only as trained, do not move a person with neck or back pain unless there is danger, and take photos and numbers. Cooperate with police.
actions: Call 112 and give your exact location.
Keep everyone away from traffic and fire risk.
Take photos and noted vehicle and driver details for police and insurance.
caution: Practice-based.

question_en: What should I tell guests to do in an earthquake?
answer: National do's and don'ts say: Drop, Cover and Hold under strong furniture during shaking. Stay inside while it shakes. Do not use lifts. If outside, move to an open area away from buildings. Afterward do not go near damaged buildings.
actions: Show guests a safe corner and an open assembly area.
Teach staff Drop, Cover and Hold.
Check gas, power and cracks after shaking before letting guests inside.
caution: Follow official local alerts.
verify_with: State Disaster Management Authority / District Disaster Management Authority

question_en: Heavy rain is coming in the hills. What should I do for guests?
answer: Follow the do's and don'ts from NIDM: know your safe route and shelter, keep dry food and boiled water ready and turn off the main power before water enters. Do not walk or drive through water of unknown depth. For landslides, listen for cracking trees or rumbling and move away quickly. Do not go near a landslide area after it.
actions: Check IMD warnings every day in monsoon.
Tell guests to stay inside or leave early if warned.
Keep a list of safe routes, shelters and phone numbers.
caution: Do not let guests drive on landslide roads in rain at night. Follow district orders.
evidence: NIDM do's and don'ts and IMD apps

question_en: What should we do when lightning or a cyclone warning comes?
answer: For lightning: unplug electronics, do not stand under trees, crouch low with feet together if caught outside, and and call 112 and give first aid to a person who is struck. For cyclone: stay indoors in the strongest part, keep away from windows and wait for official all-clear. Do not go to the sea.
actions: Download Damini Lightning for alerts.
Move guests indoors early and call them off outdoor activities.
Wait for the all-clear before going out after a cyclone.
caution: Follow official local orders. Get a doctor for anyone struck by lightning.
evidence: NIDM do's and don'ts; IMD apps

question_en: Which free government apps show weather warnings?
answer: IMD lists apps: Mausam (weather), Meghdoot Agro (advisories for farmers), Damini Lightning (lightning alerts) and UMANG (government services). They give district warnings and nowcasts. Check them before sending guests out.
actions: Install Mausam and Damini on your phone.
Check district warnings each morning in monsoon and winter.
Use the warning to reschedule or cancel activities.
caution: Apps can fail in poor network. Keep a radio or neighbour contact too.

question_en: When should I cancel a trek or send guests out because of weather?
answer: Cancel outdoor activities when an official warning is for your district, a river is rising, or roads are unsafe. Tell guests early, in writing, and offer a refund or new dates. Leave in daylight and keep a check list of all guests.
actions: Check IMD and district alerts and stop risky activities.
Tell guests the plan early and help them move before roads close.
Count everyone at the assembly point and call 112 if someone is missing.
caution: Do not overrule local administration orders.

question_en: Our village forest is used by the community. Can tourists use it? Who decides?
answer: The Forest Rights Act 2006 recognises community forest resource rights. The Gram Sabha has a central role in recognising rights and managing the forest. Using the forest for tourism usually needs the Gram Sabha's agreement and, in many cases, the Forest Department's. Rules differ by state and forest type.
actions: Hold a Gram Sabha discussion before planning forest visits.
Ask the Forest Department what permission is needed.
Write down how tourism income is shared.
caution: Never lead guests into reserved forest or protected areas without written permission.
verify_with: Gram Sabha / Forest Department / Tribal Welfare Department

question_en: We live in a Scheduled (tribal) area. Does the Gram Sabha have a say in tourism projects?
answer: In Scheduled Areas the PESA Act 1996 gives Gram Sabhas powers, for example to prevent land alienation and over minor forest produce. State PESA rules differ. Land in many Scheduled Areas cannot simply be sold or leased to non-tribal people, so ask the District Collector before any lease to an outside operator.
actions: Ask the Gram Sabha to discuss and record any tourism plan.
Check with the Tribal Welfare Department before leasing land to outsiders.
Get an agreement in writing with the Gram Sabha's consent.
caution: Land transfer rules are not verified here. Seek legal help.
evidence: S105 secondary overview; land transfer rule not verified
verify_with: Gram Sabha / District Collector / Tribal Welfare Department

question_en: Can guests feed monkeys or deer? Can we sell horns, skins or feathers?
answer: The Wild Life (Protection) Act 1972 bans hunting, which includes capturing, poisoning or trapping wild animals, and gives heavy penalties for protected animals. Do not sell wild animal products such as horns, skins or feathers. Feeding or touching wild animals is unsafe and may be banned locally. Ask the forest office.
actions: Tell guests not to feed or chase wild animals.
Do not buy, sell or display wild animal products.
Report poaching to the forest department or police.
caution: Penalties can be severe. Entry into national parks and sanctuaries needs permission.

question_en: A guest wants to fly a drone near my village. Is this allowed?
answer: Drone Rules 2021 set green, yellow and red zones. A PIB explainer says no permission is needed in a green zone up to 400 feet, yellow zones need air traffic control permission, and red zones need Central Government permission. Penalties are up to Rs 1 lakh. Always check the Digital Sky map, and never fly near defence, border, airports or crowds.
actions: Ask guests to check the Digital Sky platform for the zone.
Ban drones in sacred, wildlife and border places without permission.
Ask the police before drones at events.
caution: Rules may have changed since 2022. Wildlife and local bans also apply. Confirm.
verify_with: Digital Sky platform / DGCA / local police

question_en: Our village is near a sanctuary. What permits do I need for treks or guided walks?
answer: Rules for areas near national parks and sanctuaries (called eco-sensitive zones) differ from place to place, and entry to protected areas needs Forest Department permission. This was not verified for any area here. Ask the Divisional Forest Officer in writing.
actions: Ask the Forest Range office what treks and guides are allowed.
Use only licensed guides in protected areas.
Keep the written permission with you.
caution: Do not take guests in without a permit.

question_en: Can guests or we collect wild plants, herbs or seeds?
answer: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 regulates access to wild biological resources and sharing of benefits with local people. Commercial collection can need approval from the State Biodiversity Board. Ask your Biodiversity Management Committee or Board before any commercial plant collection. Guests should not pick plants. This was not verified on the Act in this session.
actions: Ask your Gram Panchayat if a Biodiversity Management Committee exists.
Do not allow guests to pick or take plants and seeds.
Ask the State Biodiversity Board before selling wild herbs.
caution: Verify with the Board.
evidence: Act named from general knowledge; details not read
verify_with: State Biodiversity Board / Biodiversity Management Committee

question_en: Can I sell old items, brass or antique crafts to tourists? Can they take them abroad?
answer: The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 controls dealing in and exporting antiquities (generally objects over 100 years old). Do not sell old temple, ritual or archaeological items. New handmade crafts are different. Ask the Archaeological Survey of India before selling old objects.
actions: Do not sell sacred or very old items.
Tell guests that old items cannot be taken abroad without permission.
Ask the ASI office when in doubt.
caution: The 100-year definition was not verified in this session.
evidence: Act named from general knowledge; details not verified
verify_with: Archaeological Survey of India / District Collector

question_en: Can a company copy our folk song, design or craft name? How do we protect it?
answer: A Geographical Indication (GI) tag is for products from a place, such as a famous craft, and is registered by an association of producers. It lasts ten years and can be renewed. Folk art and songs are also protected by copyright in some cases. Form a group, document your work and ask a GI or IP support centre.
actions: Form a producers' group and keep records of your craft and history.
Ask the District Industries Centre or state IP cell about a GI application.
Use only agreed names and credit makers when selling.
caution: Details on copyright for traditional works were not verified.
evidence: General knowledge; GI Act overview read but not cited
verify_with: State IPR cell / District Industries Centre

question_en: Do I have to make my homestay accessible for disabled guests?
answer: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (section 46) says service providers, government or private, must provide services according to the accessibility rules the Government frames, within two years of those rules. How this applies to a small homestay was not verified. Small steps help any guest: a ground-floor room, ramp, wide door and grab bars.
actions: Offer a ground-floor room with a step-free entrance if you can.
Fit a grab bar and a seat in one bathroom.
Ask guests about needs when they book.
caution: Do not refuse a guest because of disability. Ask the State Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities what applies.
verify_with: State Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities / District Social Welfare Office

question_en: I have a dispute with a neighbour or guest. Is there a free way to settle it without court?
answer: Lok Adalats are community-style settlement forums run by legal services authorities, and settlements are often free of court fee. Ask the District Legal Services Authority. Gram Panchayat elders can also help talk things through, but serious crimes must go to the police.
actions: Try a calm talk with elders present and write down what is agreed.
Ask the District Legal Services Authority for free legal aid or Lok Adalat.
Report serious crimes to the police.
caution: Lok Adalat details were not verified on an official page in this session. Confirm.
evidence: NALSA page listed Lok Adalat service; details not verified

question_en: What do I do if a guest dies or is seriously injured at my place?
answer: Call 112 and the ambulance at once. Give first aid if you are able. Do not move the body unless needed for safety and do not clean the room. Keep other guests calm, inform the police, and write down what happened. Tell family when police advise.
actions: Call 112 and the ambulance and follow instructions.
Keep the room and the guest's things as they are for police.
Write a clear note of times and what you saw.
caution: Do not guess the cause and do not hide anything.
